content: Participants who answered yes to either of the two questions were categorized as having a disability. To evaluate self-rated health status, participants were asked, Would you say that in general your health is excellent, very good, good, fair, or poor? The racial and ethnic categories included in this analysis were White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, and American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN). Data from the years 2004, 2005, and 2006 were combined to ensure sufficient statistical power for analyzing populations with low representation. Weighted population estimates were calculated by averaging the final weights for each year during 2004–2006. The data were adjusted to account for unequal probabilities of selection, nonresponse, and telephone noncoverage, ensuring consistency with population data and enabling accurate population estimates. Black and Hispanic adults were more likely to report their general health as fair or poor compared to White adults. Additionally, the prevalence of disability was found to be higher among Black individuals and AI/AN populations. To estimate differences in self-rated health status by race/ethnicity and disability, the CDC analyzed data from the 2004–2006 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) surveys. Efforts to reduce racial and ethnic health disparities should explicitly include strategies to improve the health and well-being of individuals with disabilities within each racial and ethnic group. These efforts must ensure that persons with disabilities have access to appropriate, available, and accessible healthcare and wellness promotion services. Accurate and timely data on the prevalence of HIV infection in the United States are essential for planning disease prevention, evaluating programs, and allocating resources. However, overall HIV prevalence cannot be directly measured because some individuals with HIV remain undiagnosed or unreported. National HIV prevalence data are incomplete due to the recent implementation of name-based HIV reporting systems in all states as of April 2008. The introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapies (HAART) has delayed the progression of HIV to AIDS and reduced AIDS-related mortality, making earlier back-calculation methods for estimating HIV prevalence based on AIDS cases unreliable. By 2006, an extended back-calculation method was used to estimate HIV prevalence more accurately, incorporating data from states with name-based HIV reporting. At the end of 2006, an estimated 1,106,400 individuals in the United States were living with diagnosed or undiagnosed HIV infection. Among these, 48% were men who have sex with men (MSM). The prevalence rate was highest among Black men and women, with rates significantly exceeding those of other racial and ethnic groups. Efforts to increase the percentage of HIV-infected individuals who are diagnosed and linked to effective care and prevention services are critical to reducing new HIV infections over time. The CDC has focused resources on increasing HIV testing, particularly among disproportionately affected populations, such as Black individuals, Hispanics, and MSM of all races. Expanding culturally appropriate opportunities for HIV testing, diagnosis, and access to early treatment and prevention services is key to reducing new infections and ultimately decreasing HIV prevalence in the United States. Rabies control in the United States has been successful due to vaccination programs and stray animal control, leading to the elimination of the canine rabies virus variant associated with dog-to-dog transmission. However, on June 18, 2008, a mixed-breed dog imported from Iraq was confirmed to have rabies. The dog was part of a shipment of 24 dogs and two cats brought to the United States as part of an international animal rescue operation. The infected dog exhibited clinical signs of rabies and was euthanized. Rabies was confirmed as a variant associated with dogs in the Middle East. The remaining animals in the shipment were distributed to 16 states, and public health investigations were initiated to identify potential human and animal exposures. The CDC recommended immediate vaccination and a six-month quarantine for all animals in the shipment due to the lack of verifiable rabies vaccination history. State health departments were notified, and 28 individuals were evaluated for potential rabies exposure, with 13 receiving postexposure prophylaxis (PEP). All animals were located and monitored during the quarantine period, with no clinical signs of rabies reported. This incident highlights the importance of public education on rabies prevention, particularly when traveling to rabies-endemic areas. Travelers should avoid contact with stray animals and ensure proper veterinary assessments and vaccinations for any adopted animals. The CDC administers federal regulations for the importation of dogs, requiring confinement and vaccination for unvaccinated animals. Recent trends indicate an increase in the importation of animals for commercial purposes, prompting the CDC to update its regulations. Continued vigilance and collaboration between federal and state agencies, health professionals, and pet importers are essential to prevent the reemergence of canine rabies virus variants in the United States.
